topic: Why database uniqueness is the final guard for idempotent request races
tomorrowTopic: Java records as immutable API boundary types

hook.headline: Idempotency needs a durable invariant
hook.hook: Application checks can coordinate retries, but only a database constraint can make duplicate key ownership impossible at the storage boundary.
hook.visualCaption: Many retries may arrive; one idempotency key may own one durable outcome.
hook.microExample: same key × 2 → UNIQUE constraint → one winner

mentalModel.title: Coordinate in code, enforce in data
mentalModel.coreIdea: An idempotency flow is strongest when application logic decides how to replay or reject a retry while PostgreSQL enforces that only one row can claim the idempotency key within the chosen scope.
mentalModel.keyOutcome: Correctness comes from the combination: application semantics define retry behavior; the database protects the single-owner invariant under races.
mentalModel.mentalShortcut: code chooses behavior; constraint protects ownership

code.title: Make key ownership explicit
code.intro: Model the invariant in PostgreSQL instead of relying on a prior existence check that can race.
code.code:
CREATE TABLE idempotency_record (
  client_id bigint NOT NULL,
  idem_key text NOT NULL,
  resource_id bigint,
  response_status integer,
  UNIQUE (client_id, idem_key)
);
code.highlightReason: The composite unique constraint defines the durable ownership rule and lets PostgreSQL arbitrate concurrent claims for the same scoped key.
code.takeaway: A read-then-insert check is not itself a concurrency guarantee; the uniqueness rule belongs in the database schema.
code.professionalNote: Choose the constraint scope deliberately. A globally unique key and a per-client unique key express different API contracts, so the schema must match the idempotency-key semantics you expose.

production.title: Separate invariant from retry policy
production.scenario: Two identical POST requests with the same idempotency key reach different application instances at nearly the same time.
problems: Both instances can observe that no key row exists before either insert commits.
Without a uniqueness invariant, both requests may proceed to create separate business resources.
production.professionalApproach: Let both requests attempt the same constrained key claim inside an appropriate transaction boundary. Treat the database-enforced duplicate claim as a concurrency outcome, then load or wait for the canonical stored result according to your API design. Keep the business write and idempotency state coordinated so the recorded outcome cannot point to a resource that was never committed.
production.debugClue: If duplicate resources exist despite idempotency keys, inspect the actual unique constraint, its scope, and whether resource creation can commit independently of the idempotency record.

interview.question: Why is a database unique constraint still necessary if the service checks whether an idempotency key already exists?
interview.answer: Because the existence check and insert are separate operations unless protected by a stronger concurrency mechanism. Two requests can both observe absence and then both try to claim the key. A PostgreSQL unique constraint makes the single-owner rule durable and lets the database reject one competing claim. The service still owns the API semantics: it decides how to translate that concurrency outcome into replaying the stored result, waiting, or returning another documented response.
